source.text: Ἀδελφοί, ἐὰν καὶ προλημφθῇ ἄνθρωπος ἔν τινι παραπτώματι, ὑμεῖς οἱ πνευματικοὶ καταρτίζετε τὸν τοιοῦτον ἐν πνεύματι πραΰτητος, σκοπῶν σεαυτόν, μὴ καὶ σὺ πειρασθῇς.

records.literal_gloss: Brothers, if even is overtaken a man in some trespass, you the spiritual [ones] restore the such [one] in a spirit of gentleness, watching yourself, lest also you be tempted.

en.L: {{gender:Brothers and sisters|Brothers}}, if someone is even caught in some wrongdoing, you who are spiritual, restore such a one in a spirit of gentleness, keeping watch on yourself, so that you also are not tempted.
en.B: {{gender:Brothers and sisters|Brothers}}, suppose someone is caught out in some wrongdoing. You who are spiritual must set that person right again, and do it with a gentle spirit. Keep an eye on yourself as you do, in case you are tempted too.
en.R: {{gender:Brothers and sisters|Brothers}}, someone among you may be found doing something wrong. If that happens, you whose lives are guided by the Spirit should help that person back onto the right path. Be gentle about it. And watch out for yourself, so that you are not tempted as well.

decisions.choice: caught: taken by surprise in the act, found out
alternatives: overtaken: carried away by a sin before the person can resist
decisions.reason: προλαμβάνω means to take or seize beforehand, and with καὶ ("even") the clause most naturally pictures someone surprised or found out in the act. The other sense, being overtaken by sin before one sees it coming, is also possible. Either way the person has really done wrong, and the point is how the church responds.

decisions.choice: the spiritual: those who live by the Spirit, as 5:16-25 has described
alternatives: a spiritual elite within the church
said with irony, of those who think themselves spiritual
decisions.reason: πνευματικοὶ picks up the Spirit language of 5:16-25: walking by the Spirit, led by the Spirit, bearing the Spirit's fruit. Paul is addressing every believer who lives that way, not a special class. Some hear a touch of irony aimed at people who prided themselves on being spiritual, but nothing in the sentence requires it.

decisions.choice: restore: set right, mend what is broken
decisions.reason: καταρτίζω is used of mending nets (Mark 1:19) and of putting things into proper order. The aim is to bring the person back, not to punish.

decisions.choice: a spirit of gentleness: a gentle attitude, the gentleness the Spirit produces
alternatives: the Holy Spirit, who gives gentleness
decisions.reason: πνεύματι here most naturally means a person's attitude, as in 1 Corinthians 4:21. Gentleness, πραΰτης, is one of the fruit of the Spirit in 5:23, so the Spirit stands behind the attitude even if the word does not name him directly.

decisions.choice: Paul turns from "you" plural to "you" singular: each helper must watch himself or herself
alternatives: the singular is only a change of style
decisions.reason: After the plural command, σκοπῶν σεαυτόν and σὺ are singular. Paul presses the warning on each person individually: anyone who helps another out of a fault can fall into the same or another temptation.

decisions.choice: {{gender:Brothers and sisters|Brothers}}
decisions.reason: Paul is writing to all the believers in Galatia, women and men (3:28). Traditional is one tap away.

decisions.choice: wrongdoing (B); doing something wrong (R)
decisions.reason: "Trespass" now mostly means entering private land; plain words say what the Greek word means, a false step, a wrong act.

decisions.choice: you whose lives are guided by the Spirit
decisions.reason: Readable says what "spiritual" means here (m2), using the language of 5:16-18.

source.text: ἀλλήλων τὰ βάρη βαστάζετε, καὶ οὕτως ἀναπληρώσετε τὸν νόμον τοῦ Χριστοῦ.

records.literal_gloss: Of one another the burdens bear, and thus you will fulfill the law of the Christ.

en.L: Bear the burdens of one another, and in this way you will fulfill the law of the {{christos:Christ|Messiah}}.
en.B: Take up one another's heavy loads, and so you will fulfill the law of {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}}.
en.R: Help each other carry the things that weigh you down. When you do, you will be doing all that the law of {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} asks.

decisions.choice: burdens: heavy loads, anything too heavy for a person to carry alone
alternatives: only the moral failures of verse 1
decisions.reason: βάρη are weights that press a person down. Coming just after verse 1, they include the weight of sin and temptation, but the word is general and covers any hardship a fellow believer is struggling under.

decisions.choice: the law of Christ: the command to love, as Christ taught and lived it
alternatives: a new code of rules given by Christ
the law of Moses as Christ interprets it
decisions.reason: Paul has just said that the whole law is fulfilled in one word, "love your neighbor as yourself" (5:14), and has described Christ as the one who loved him and gave himself for him (2:20). Bearing others' burdens is that love put into practice. The phrase is pointed in a letter where the opponents urge the Galatians to take on the law of Moses: the law believers live by is Christ's. Paul uses a similar phrase in 1 Corinthians 9:21.

decisions.choice: follow SBLGNT: "you will fulfill", a future
decisions.reason: Many manuscripts read a command, "and so fulfill the law of Christ"; the two forms differ by a single letter. SBLGNT reads the future ἀναπληρώσετε, a promise of what carrying burdens achieves. The sense is close either way. Reviewers should check the apparatus.

decisions.choice: {{christos:Christ|Messiah}} (L); {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} (B, R)
decisions.reason: Title setting. Literal keeps the article.

decisions.choice: you will be doing all that the law of Christ asks
alternatives: you will fulfill the law of Christ
decisions.reason: Readable says plainly what "fulfill" means: to do in full what the law requires.

source.text: εἰ γὰρ δοκεῖ τις εἶναί τι μηδὲν ὤν, φρεναπατᾷ ἑαυτόν·

records.literal_gloss: For if thinks anyone to be something, nothing being, he deceives himself;

en.L: For if anyone thinks [{{gender:themselves|himself}}] to be something while being nothing, {{gender:they deceive themselves|he deceives himself}}.
en.B: For those who think they are something when they are nothing are only fooling themselves.
en.R: People who think they are too important to help others are fooling themselves. In fact they are nothing.

decisions.choice: for: the reason why some will not bear others' burdens
decisions.reason: γὰρ ties the verse to verses 1-2. Pride, thinking oneself above a fallen brother or sister, is what keeps a person from stooping to help, and it is the danger verse 1 warns of.

decisions.choice: while being nothing: no one has standing of their own before God
alternatives: only those who are proud are nothing
decisions.reason: μηδὲν ὤν could describe the proud person in particular, but Paul's point is wider: no one is "something" in himself or herself (compare 2:6; 1 Corinthians 3:7). To think otherwise is to deceive oneself.

decisions.choice: {{gender:they deceive themselves|he deceives himself}} (L); plural "those", "people" (B, R)
decisions.reason: "Anyone" includes women and men. Literal keeps the singular with the gender setting; Balanced and Readable make the sentence plural so that no pronoun is needed.

decisions.choice: think they are too important to help others
decisions.reason: Readable makes the link with verses 1-2 explicit (m1).

source.text: τὸ δὲ ἔργον ἑαυτοῦ δοκιμαζέτω ἕκαστος, καὶ τότε εἰς ἑαυτὸν μόνον τὸ καύχημα ἕξει καὶ οὐκ εἰς τὸν ἕτερον, ἕκαστος γὰρ τὸ ἴδιον φορτίον βαστάσει.

records.literal_gloss: But the work of himself let test each [one], and then as to himself alone the boast he will have and not as to the other; \v 5 for each the own load will carry.

en.L: But let each one test {{gender:their|his}} own work, and then {{gender:they|he}} will have [a ground for] boasting with regard to {{gender:themselves|himself}} alone, and not with regard to the other [person]; \v 5 for each one will carry {{gender:their|his}} own load.
en.B: Each of you should examine your own conduct. Then any pride you take will be in what you yourself have done, not in how you compare with someone else. \v 5 For each of you will have your own load to carry.
en.R: Each of you should look carefully at what you yourself are doing. Then if you have something to be proud of, it will be your own work, and not that you look better than someone else. \v 5 Each of you will have your own load to carry.

decisions.choice: test: examine one's own work to see whether it is genuine
decisions.reason: δοκιμάζω is used for testing metal to prove it is genuine. Instead of measuring others, each person is to examine his or her own conduct (ἔργον, "work", meaning the whole of what one does).

decisions.choice: a person's boast is to rest on his or her own work, not on comparison with someone else
alternatives: boasting is kept private, to oneself
decisions.reason: The two phrases with εἰς set out what the boast is measured against: oneself alone, not the other person. Paul is not encouraging pride; he rules out the kind of pride that comes from feeling superior to someone who has fallen (verses 1-3). The same word for boasting returns in verses 13-14, where Paul's only boast is the cross.

decisions.choice: load: the burden of responsibility that belongs to each person
alternatives: the same thing as the burdens of verse 2
decisions.reason: φορτίον is a different word from βάρη in verse 2. There is no contradiction: believers help one another with burdens too heavy to carry alone, while each remains answerable for his or her own life. Jesus uses the same word for a load in Matthew 11:30.

decisions.choice: will carry: likely looking ahead to God's judgment
alternatives: a general truth about life now
decisions.reason: The future βαστάσει may simply state a rule, but with "reap" in verses 7-9 it most likely looks forward to the day when each person gives account to God (Romans 14:12). The text does not decide between the two.

decisions.choice: each of you ... your own
alternatives: let each one test his own work
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable address the reader directly, which keeps the sense of "each" without a third-person pronoun.

decisions.choice: pride you take (B); something to be proud of (R)
decisions.reason: In current English "boast" is always bad, but here the boast that rests on one's own tested work is not condemned (m2). Literal keeps "boasting".

decisions.choice: {{gender:their|his}} own, {{gender:themselves|himself}}
decisions.reason: Each person is meant, women and men; Literal keeps the singular with the gender setting.

source.text: Κοινωνείτω δὲ ὁ κατηχούμενος τὸν λόγον τῷ κατηχοῦντι ἐν πᾶσιν ἀγαθοῖς.

records.literal_gloss: Let share now the [one] being taught the word with the [one] teaching in all good things.

en.L: Now let the one who is taught the word share in all good things with the one who teaches.
en.B: Those who are being taught the word must share all their good things with the one who teaches them.
en.R: If someone teaches you God's message, share with that teacher all the good things you have.

decisions.choice: the one taught and the one teaching: a learner and a teacher of the Christian message
decisions.reason: κατηχέω is the word for instruction by word of mouth. λόγον is "the word", the message of the gospel, so this is about those who teach the faith in the church.

decisions.choice: share all good things: support the teacher, especially with material help
alternatives: the teacher and the taught share all good things together
decisions.reason: κοινωνέω means to have a share, a partnership. Paul elsewhere argues that those who teach the gospel should be supported by those they teach (1 Corinthians 9:11, 14; Romans 15:27). "All good things" is wider than money, but includes it, and verses 9-10 go on to doing good.

decisions.choice: now: a new instruction, loosely linked to what precedes
decisions.reason: δὲ can mark contrast: each carries his or her own load, but the learner should share with the teacher. It more likely marks a new point in a list of practical instructions.

decisions.choice: God's message
decisions.reason: Readable says whose word is being taught (m1).

source.text: μὴ πλανᾶσθε, θεὸς οὐ μυκτηρίζεται· ὃ γὰρ ἐὰν σπείρῃ ἄνθρωπος, τοῦτο καὶ θερίσει·

records.literal_gloss: Not be misled, God not is mocked; for whatever if sows a man, this also he will reap;

en.L: Do not be led astray; God is not mocked. For whatever {{gender:a person|a man}} sows, that {{gender:they|he}} will also reap.
en.B: Do not let anyone mislead you: God is not to be sneered at. Whatever people sow, that is what they will reap.
en.R: Do not fool yourselves. No one can sneer at God and get away with it. People will harvest whatever they plant.

decisions.choice: do not be misled: do not deceive yourselves or let others deceive you
decisions.reason: πλανᾶσθε can be passive ("do not be led astray") or middle ("do not deceive yourselves"). Both fit: Paul has warned of self-deception in verse 3 and of the people misleading them throughout the letter (1:7; 5:10).

decisions.choice: God is not sneered at: no one treats God with contempt and escapes the outcome
decisions.reason: μυκτηρίζω means to turn up one's nose, to sneer at. People may live as though God's warnings do not matter, but they will not get away with it. The saying that follows explains why.

decisions.choice: sowing and reaping: what a person does decides what follows from it
decisions.reason: The farming picture was a common proverb (Job 4:8; Proverbs 22:8; Hosea 8:7; 2 Corinthians 9:6). Verse 8 applies it: what is sown into the flesh and what is sown into the Spirit bring two different harvests.

decisions.choice: {{gender:a person|a man}} ... {{gender:they|he}}
decisions.reason: The proverb is about anyone; Literal keeps the singular with the gender setting, and Balanced and Readable make it plural.

decisions.choice: No one can sneer at God and get away with it
decisions.reason: Readable says what the short saying means (m2).

decisions.choice: plant, harvest
decisions.reason: "Sow" and "reap" are less common words for younger readers; Readable uses plain farming words and keeps the picture.

source.text: ὅτι ὁ σπείρων εἰς τὴν σάρκα ἑαυτοῦ ἐκ τῆς σαρκὸς θερίσει φθοράν, ὁ δὲ σπείρων εἰς τὸ πνεῦμα ἐκ τοῦ πνεύματος θερίσει ζωὴν αἰώνιον.

records.literal_gloss: For the [one] sowing to the flesh of himself, from the flesh will reap decay, but the [one] sowing to the Spirit, from the Spirit will reap life eternal.

en.L: For the one who sows to {{gender:their|his}} own flesh will reap decay from the flesh, but the one who sows to the Spirit will reap eternal life from the Spirit.
en.B: Those who sow into their own flesh will gather a harvest of decay from the flesh; those who sow into the Spirit will gather from the Spirit a harvest of eternal life.
en.R: If you plant to satisfy your own sinful desires, the harvest they give you will be ruin. But if you plant what the Spirit wants, the Spirit will give you a harvest of eternal life.

decisions.choice: flesh: the sinful human self that opposes the Spirit, as in 5:13-24
alternatives: reliance on circumcision and the law
decisions.reason: σάρκα is set against πνεῦμα, as flesh and Spirit are set against each other in 5:16-17. Sowing to one's flesh is living for the desires listed in 5:19-21. Some hear an allusion to circumcision too, since verses 12-13 speak of boasting in the flesh, but the word "own" points to a person's own sinful self.

decisions.choice: decay: corruption that ends in ruin and death
decisions.reason: φθοράν is the decay of what perishes (Romans 8:21; 1 Corinthians 15:42). It stands opposite eternal life: the harvest of the flesh rots away, while the Spirit's harvest lasts.

decisions.choice: the Spirit: God's Holy Spirit
decisions.reason: Unlike the flesh, the Spirit is not called the person's "own". It is the Spirit of 5:16-25, who gives life (5:25) and whose fruit is listed in 5:22-23.

decisions.choice: gather a harvest (B); harvest (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable spell out the farming picture so that the two harvests stand side by side.

decisions.choice: your own sinful desires
decisions.reason: Readable says what "flesh" means here (m1), as in chapter 5.

decisions.choice: if you plant
decisions.reason: Readable addresses the reader directly to keep the sentence short.

source.text: τὸ δὲ καλὸν ποιοῦντες μὴ ἐγκακῶμεν, καιρῷ γὰρ ἰδίῳ θερίσομεν μὴ ἐκλυόμενοι.

records.literal_gloss: And the good doing not let us grow weary, for in time own we will reap, not giving up.

en.L: And let us not lose heart in doing what is good, for in [its] own time we will reap, if we do not grow slack.
en.B: We must not tire of doing good. When the right time comes we will bring in the harvest, as long as we do not slacken.
en.R: So let us not get tired of doing good things. If we keep going and do not quit, we will have a harvest when the time is right.

decisions.choice: in its own time: the time God has set, the final harvest
alternatives: sooner or later in this life
decisions.reason: καιρῷ ἰδίῳ is "the proper time", the time that belongs to the harvest. After the eternal life of verse 8, it most naturally means the day God has fixed for gathering the harvest, though good may also come of good deeds sooner.

decisions.choice: if we do not give up: a condition for reaping
alternatives: describing the harvest: we will reap without growing weary
decisions.reason: The participle ἐκλυόμενοι most likely states a condition: the harvest comes to those who do not slacken. It repeats the warning of the first clause.

decisions.choice: If we keep going and do not quit, we will have a harvest
alternatives: we will reap, if we do not give up
decisions.reason: Readable puts the condition first, which is easier to follow.

source.text: ἄρα οὖν ὡς καιρὸν ἔχομεν, ἐργαζώμεθα τὸ ἀγαθὸν πρὸς πάντας, μάλιστα δὲ πρὸς τοὺς οἰκείους τῆς πίστεως.

records.literal_gloss: So then as opportunity we have, let us work the good toward all, especially now toward the members of the household of the faith.

en.L: So then, while we have opportunity, let us work what is good toward all [people], and especially toward those of the household of the faith.
en.B: So whenever we have the chance, we should do good to everyone, and above all to those who belong to the family of faith.
en.R: So whenever we have the chance, let us do good to everyone, and most of all to our fellow believers, the family that shares our faith.

decisions.choice: as we have opportunity: whenever, and while, the time is ours
decisions.reason: ὡς with καιρὸν can mean "whenever" or "while". καιρός is the same word as "time" in verse 9: the harvest has its time, and the present is the time for sowing. Both senses are present: every chance that comes, while it lasts.

decisions.choice: the household of the faith: fellow believers, God's family
decisions.reason: οἰκείους means members of a household. Paul pictures believers as one family (compare Ephesians 2:19), bound together by the faith they share. They have a first claim, but not the only claim, on one another's help.

decisions.choice: family
decisions.reason: "Household" is now a formal word; "family" keeps the picture. Literal keeps "household".

decisions.choice: our fellow believers, the family that shares our faith
decisions.reason: Readable names the people meant and keeps the key word "faith".

source.text: Ἴδετε πηλίκοις ὑμῖν γράμμασιν ἔγραψα τῇ ἐμῇ χειρί.

records.literal_gloss: See with how large to you letters I wrote with the my hand.

en.L: See with what large letters I have written to you with my own hand.
en.B: Notice what large letters I make as I write to you in my own hand.
en.R: Now I am writing to you myself, in my own handwriting. Look how big the letters are!

decisions.choice: Paul takes the pen from his scribe to write the end of the letter himself
alternatives: Paul wrote the whole letter by hand
decisions.reason: Letters were usually dictated to a scribe (Romans 16:22), and the sender often added the last lines himself to show that the letter was genuine (1 Corinthians 16:21; Colossians 4:18; 2 Thessalonians 3:17). It is likely that this is the point where Paul's own hand begins.

decisions.choice: I have written: a letter-writer's past tense, meaning "I am writing"
alternatives: looking back over the whole letter
decisions.reason: Writers of letters often used the past tense ἔγραψα from the point of view of the reader, for whom the writing is past when the letter arrives. Here it most likely refers to these closing lines.

decisions.choice: large letters: written large for emphasis
alternatives: large because Paul could not see well (compare 4:15)
large because he was not a trained scribe
decisions.reason: πηλίκοις is "how large", not "how long": Paul is speaking of the size of the letters, not the length of the letter. Large writing draws the eye, as underlining does, to the summary that follows. Other reasons have been suggested, such as poor eyesight; the text does not say.

decisions.choice: Now I am writing to you myself, in my own handwriting. Look how big the letters are!
decisions.reason: Readable explains the change of hand (m1, m2) before the call to look.

source.text: ὅσοι θέλουσιν εὐπροσωπῆσαι ἐν σαρκί, οὗτοι ἀναγκάζουσιν ὑμᾶς περιτέμνεσθαι, μόνον ἵνα τῷ σταυρῷ τοῦ Χριστοῦ μὴ διώκωνται·

records.literal_gloss: As many as want to make a good showing in flesh, these compel you to be circumcised, only so that for the cross of the Christ they may not be persecuted;

en.L: As many as want to make a good showing in [the] flesh, these are trying to compel you to be circumcised, only so that they may not be persecuted for the cross of the {{christos:Christ|Messiah}}.
en.B: The people who want to make a fine impression in the flesh are the ones pressing you to be circumcised. They have one motive: they do not want to suffer persecution because of the cross of {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}}.
en.R: Some people want to look good because of what has been done to their bodies. They are the ones trying to force you to be circumcised. They have only one reason: they do not want to be persecuted for holding to the message of the cross of {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}}.

decisions.choice: make a good showing in the flesh: win approval by an outward mark in the body
alternatives: look good by human standards in general
decisions.reason: εὐπροσωπέω means to put on a good face. "In the flesh" here points to circumcision, a mark cut in the body (verse 13), which would make them look respectable to those who prized it.

decisions.choice: are trying to compel: the pressure is real, but the Galatians have not yet given in
decisions.reason: The present ἀναγκάζουσιν describes ongoing pressure. Paul used the same verb of Titus, who was not compelled to be circumcised (2:3), and of Peter compelling Gentiles to live like Jews (2:14).

decisions.choice: persecuted for the cross: opposed by those who saw a gospel without circumcision as abandoning God's law
decisions.reason: Paul says he himself is persecuted because he does not preach circumcision; if he did, "the offense of the cross" would be removed (5:11). A message that Christ crucified is enough, without the law, drew hostility from many of Paul's fellow Jews (1:13; 4:29). The dative σταυρῷ gives the cause.

decisions.choice: these: the teachers troubling the Galatians
decisions.reason: οὗτοι points back to the people who are unsettling the churches (1:7; 5:10, 12). Paul now gives his own judgment on their motives.

decisions.choice: {{christos:Christ|Messiah}} (L); {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} (B, R)
decisions.reason: Title setting. Literal keeps the article.

decisions.choice: for holding to the message of the cross
decisions.reason: Readable says that the persecution is for the message of the cross, not for the wooden cross itself (m3).

decisions.choice: because of what has been done to their bodies
decisions.reason: Readable says what "flesh" refers to here (m1).

source.text: οὐδὲ γὰρ οἱ περιτεμνόμενοι αὐτοὶ νόμον φυλάσσουσιν, ἀλλὰ θέλουσιν ὑμᾶς περιτέμνεσθαι ἵνα ἐν τῇ ὑμετέρᾳ σαρκὶ καυχήσωνται.

records.literal_gloss: For not even those being circumcised themselves law keep, but they want you to be circumcised so that in your flesh they may boast.

en.L: For not even those who are circumcised themselves keep [the] law, but they want you to be circumcised so that they may boast in your flesh.
en.B: For even these circumcised people do not themselves obey the law. What they want is your circumcision, so that your flesh can be something for them to boast about.
en.R: These people are circumcised, but even they do not obey the law. They want you to be circumcised only so they can brag about what was done to your body.

decisions.choice: follow SBLGNT: those who are being circumcised (present)
decisions.reason: Some manuscripts read a perfect participle, "those who have been circumcised". SBLGNT reads περιτεμνόμενοι. Reviewers should check the apparatus.

decisions.choice: those circumcised: the teachers who insist on circumcision
alternatives: Gentile converts who have accepted circumcision
decisions.reason: The present participle could describe Gentiles who are having themselves circumcised, but the sentence goes on "they want you to be circumcised", which fits the teachers of verse 12. The present may describe them as the circumcision party.

decisions.choice: boast in your flesh: take pride in your circumcision as their success
decisions.reason: "Flesh" here is the body that bears circumcision. Paul says the teachers want the Galatians' circumcision as a trophy. Verse 14 sets his own boast, the cross, against it.

decisions.choice: what was done to your body
decisions.reason: Readable says what "flesh" refers to here (m3).

source.text: ἐμοὶ δὲ μὴ γένοιτο καυχᾶσθαι εἰ μὴ ἐν τῷ σταυρῷ τοῦ κυρίου ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ, δι’ οὗ ἐμοὶ κόσμος ἐσταύρωται κἀγὼ κόσμῳ.

records.literal_gloss: But to me may it not be to boast except in the cross of the Lord of us Jesus Christ, through which to me [the] world has been crucified and I to [the] world.

en.L: But for me, may it never be [that I] boast except in the cross of our Lord Jesus {{christos:Christ|Messiah}}, through which [the] world has been crucified to me, and I to [the] world.
en.B: But far be it from me to boast of anything except the cross of our Lord Jesus {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}}. Through that cross the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world.
en.R: But I will never brag about anything except the cross of our Lord Jesus {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}}. Because of that cross, the world and all it prizes is as dead to me as someone nailed to a cross, and I am just as dead to the world.

decisions.choice: may it never be: the strongest refusal Paul has
decisions.reason: μὴ γένοιτο is the expression Paul uses to reject something outright (2:17; 3:21). Here it is personal: the one thing he will boast in is the cross, in contrast with the teachers who boast in circumcision (verse 13).

decisions.choice: through which: through the cross
decisions.reason: The relative οὗ could refer to the cross or to the Lord Jesus Christ; the form is the same. The sentence is about the cross, and so are verse 12 and 2:19-20, so the cross is the more likely reference. The meaning is much the same either way.

decisions.choice: the world: life organized apart from God, with its standards of status and religious standing
decisions.reason: κόσμος here is "this present evil age" (1:4): its ways of ranking people, including circumcision and the marks of religious status. At the cross that world lost its claim on Paul, and he ceased to count in its eyes.

decisions.choice: crucified to each other: the cross has ended the relationship on both sides
decisions.reason: The perfect ἐσταύρωται speaks of something done and still in effect, as in 2:19, "I have been crucified with Christ". The world is dead to Paul, and Paul is dead to it.

decisions.choice: {{christos:Christ|Messiah}} (L); {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} (B, R)
decisions.reason: Title setting.

decisions.choice: the world and all it prizes is as dead to me as someone nailed to a cross, and I am just as dead to the world
alternatives: the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world
decisions.reason: Readable explains the picture of crucifixion and the sense of "world" (m3, m4).

decisions.choice: far be it from me
decisions.reason: An English expression of strong refusal that does not add God's name.

source.text: οὔτε γὰρ περιτομή τί ἐστιν οὔτε ἀκροβυστία, ἀλλὰ καινὴ κτίσις.

records.literal_gloss: For neither circumcision anything is nor uncircumcision, but a new creation.

en.L: For neither is circumcision anything, nor uncircumcision, but a new creation [is].
en.B: For circumcision is nothing, and uncircumcision is nothing; the one thing that matters is a new creation.
en.R: It does not matter whether a person is circumcised or not. What matters is being part of the new creation God is making.

decisions.choice: follow SBLGNT: "For neither circumcision ..."
alternatives: "For in Christ Jesus neither circumcision avails anything ..."
decisions.reason: Many manuscripts add "in Christ Jesus" and a verb meaning "avails", making the verse match 5:6. The shorter SBLGNT text is better supported by early manuscripts, and copyists tended to make parallel passages agree. Reviewers should check the apparatus.

decisions.choice: a new creation: the new world God has begun in Christ, and each person made new within it
alternatives: only the individual believer made new
only the renewal of the whole world
decisions.reason: καινὴ κτίσις has no article and no "anyone". In 2 Corinthians 5:17 the phrase applies to the person who is in Christ; Isaiah 65:17 speaks of new heavens and a new earth. Here, after "the world has been crucified to me", Paul probably means both: the new age that has begun in Christ, and the person who belongs to it.

decisions.choice: neither circumcision nor uncircumcision counts: being Jew or Gentile gives no standing
decisions.reason: Paul says the same in 5:6 and 1 Corinthians 7:19. Uncircumcision gives no advantage either; the Galatians should not boast of it.

decisions.choice: being part of the new creation God is making
decisions.reason: Readable names God as the one who creates and keeps both the personal and the wider sense (m2).

source.text: καὶ ὅσοι τῷ κανόνι τούτῳ στοιχήσουσιν, εἰρήνη ἐπ’ αὐτοὺς καὶ ἔλεος, καὶ ἐπὶ τὸν Ἰσραὴλ τοῦ θεοῦ.

records.literal_gloss: And as many as by the rule this will walk, peace upon them and mercy, and upon the Israel of the God.

en.L: And as many as will walk in line with this rule, peace [be] upon them, and mercy, and upon the Israel of God.
en.B: May peace and mercy be on all who live in line with this rule, and on the Israel of God.
en.R: May God give peace and mercy to everyone who lives by this rule, and to the Israel of God.

decisions.choice: walk in line with this rule: live by the standard of verse 15
decisions.reason: κανόνι is a measuring rule, a standard. The rule is what Paul has just said: what counts is not circumcision but a new creation. στοιχέω means to keep in line, as in 5:25, "let us keep in step with the Spirit".

decisions.choice: an echo of the blessing "peace upon Israel"
decisions.reason: Psalms 125:5 and 128:6 end with "peace upon Israel". Paul gives the familiar blessing to those who walk by the rule of the new creation.

decisions.choice: the Israel of God: uncertain whether this is the whole church, Jew and Gentile, or Jewish believers or Israel
alternatives: the whole people of God in Christ, Jewish and Gentile believers together
the people of Israel, for whom Paul prays for mercy
decisions.reason: The phrase occurs only here. If καὶ means "that is", the Israel of God is the same group as those who walk by this rule: all believers, who are Abraham's offspring (3:7, 29). If it means "and also", Paul adds a second group: Jewish believers, or Israel as a people, to whom God will show mercy (Romans 11:26-32). The order "peace ... and mercy" and the strong contrast with the circumcision party are argued on both sides. The grammar allows both.

decisions.choice: May peace and mercy be on ...
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable put the blessing as a prayer, as Paul's greetings are (1:3). Readable names God as the giver.

source.text: Τοῦ λοιποῦ κόπους μοι μηδεὶς παρεχέτω, ἐγὼ γὰρ τὰ στίγματα τοῦ Ἰησοῦ ἐν τῷ σώματί μου βαστάζω.

records.literal_gloss: From the rest troubles to me no one let give, for I the marks of the Jesus on the body of me bear.

en.L: From now on let no one cause me troubles, for I carry the marks of Jesus on my body.
en.B: Let no one give me any more trouble from now on, for I carry on my body the marks that show I belong to Jesus.
en.R: From now on, do not let anyone make trouble for me. The scars on my body show that I belong to Jesus.

decisions.choice: from now on
decisions.reason: Τοῦ λοιποῦ is a set phrase for time to come, "henceforth".

decisions.choice: the marks of Jesus: scars from Paul's sufferings for Jesus, which brand him as Jesus' own
alternatives: marks that share in Jesus' wounds in a mystical way
decisions.reason: στίγματα were marks branded or tattooed on slaves, soldiers or devotees of a god to show to whom they belonged. Paul carried scars from beatings and stoning (2 Corinthians 11:23-25; Acts 14:19). Those are his marks: unlike the circumcision the teachers urge, they show he belongs to Jesus, and they are the cost of preaching the cross.

decisions.choice: the marks that show I belong to Jesus (B); The scars on my body show that I belong to Jesus (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say what the marks mean (m2); Readable also says what they were.

source.text: Ἡ χάρις τοῦ κυρίου ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ μετὰ τοῦ πνεύματος ὑμῶν, ἀδελφοί· ἀμήν.

records.literal_gloss: The grace of the Lord of us Jesus Christ [be] with the spirit of you, brothers; amen.

en.L: The grace of our Lord Jesus {{christos:Christ|Messiah}} [be] with your spirit, {{gender:brothers and sisters|brothers}}. Amen.
en.B: {{gender:Brothers and sisters|Brothers}}, may the grace of our Lord Jesus {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} be with your spirit. Amen.
en.R: {{gender:Brothers and sisters|Brothers}}, may the grace of our Lord Jesus {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} be with each one of you. Amen.

decisions.choice: with your spirit: with you yourselves
alternatives: with the human spirit as distinct from the body
decisions.reason: "With your spirit" is a way of saying "with you", as in Philippians 4:23 and Philemon 25; πνεύματος here is the inner person, the whole of who they are.

decisions.choice: brothers: the last word before "amen", a warm address after a severe letter
decisions.reason: This is the only one of Paul's letters to end with ἀδελφοί. After the sharp words of the letter, he closes by calling the Galatians his family. The term includes all the believers, women and men.

decisions.choice: {{christos:Christ|Messiah}}; {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}}; {{gender:brothers and sisters|brothers}}
decisions.reason: Title setting and gender setting.

decisions.choice: {{gender:Brothers and sisters|Brothers}} first
alternatives: at the end, as in the Greek
decisions.reason: In English a direct address before "Amen" is awkward; Balanced and Readable place it first.

decisions.choice: with each one of you
decisions.reason: Readable says what the idiom means (m1).
